Medical History

- Current health concerns and risk factors: 3-day history of profuse watery diarrhoea (≈hourly), crampy mid-lower abdominal pain (~6/10, colicky), occasional nausea/vomiting (worse with milk), subjective fever; risk of dehydration identified.  
- Relevant family medical history: Father with stage-III colon cancer; brother experiencing similar diarrhoeal illness for 5 days; no other conditions mentioned.  
- Medications (including OTC or shared medications): Paracetamol (dose/route/frequency not documented); no regular prescription drugs; advised to start oral rehydration salts (Diarolyte).  
- Immunisation status reviewed: Not recorded.  
- Sexual and reproductive health: Not recorded.  
- Physical activity and nutrition: Physical activity not recorded; nutrition note—patient often buys takeaway food and currently tolerating only light/soft diet.  
- Alcohol, tobacco, and substance use: Social smoker (occasional, mainly on weekends); alcohol—1 beer on some weekdays, heavier binge 1–2×/month; advised to avoid alcohol while unwell.  
- Hearing loss or concerns: Not recorded.  
- Mood/mental health (including depression, self-harm risk): Not recorded.  
- Vision problems or recent changes: Not recorded.  
- Family and social relationships, caring responsibilities: Lives with mother and sister; works in a government office (Central London); reports difficulty attending work due to illness.

Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)

Key findings: Young male with acute onset of high-frequency watery diarrhoea, abdominal cramps, mild vomiting, and subjective fever; brother with similar illness; no blood in stool; dehydration risk.

Differential diagnoses (consistent with DDx):
• Acute viral gastroenteritis (likely norovirus) – High likelihood: abrupt onset, highly contagious, household case.  
• Acute bacterial gastroenteritis/food-borne infection – Moderate likelihood: takeaway food habit and feverish feeling; no blood noted.  
• Transient post-infectious lactose intolerance – Low-moderate likelihood: milk triggers vomiting.

Working diagnosis: Acute infective gastroenteritis (probable viral). Dehydration risk acknowledged.

Management Plan

• Oral rehydration therapy: Start over-the-counter Dioralyte; maintain clear fluids initially, progress to soft diet (soups, mashed foods) as tolerated.  
• Symptom control: Continue paracetamol for fever/pain as needed.  
• Lifestyle advice: Avoid alcohol until recovery; monitor urine output.  
• Safety-net: If no improvement or worsening (ongoing high-volume diarrhoea, inability to keep fluids down, reduced urine output) within 48 hours, patient to re-contact clinic for further assessment and possible investigations (vitals, bloods, stool culture).  
• Education: Discussed signs of dehydration and importance of fluid replacement.  
• Follow-up: Tele-review arranged in 1–2 days if symptoms persist.

Consider:

- Allied health referral (EPC – 10 visits): Not recorded.  
- Reproductive or sexual health clinic referral: Not recorded.  
- Mental health support if indicated (e.g., psychologist, AMS support): Not recorded.  
- CTG registration: Not recorded.  
- Preventive health follow-up booked (e.g., flu vaccine, Pap test): Not recorded.  

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx):

1. Acute viral gastroenteritis – High: classic presentation, contact with symptomatic brother.  
2. Acute bacterial gastroenteritis – Moderate: similar symptoms; dietary exposures possible.  
3. Transient lactose intolerance – Low-moderate: dairy precipitates vomiting; could be post-infective.

Quality checks (always include at bottom of note):

● Missing expected elements: objective vitals (BP, pulse, temperature), weight/BMI, immunisation review, physical examination findings, urinalysis, mental health screening, detailed alcohol/smoking quantification, comprehensive diet and exercise review.  
● No contradictions noted between transcript and DDx.  
● Transcript quality: Audio clear but video absent; no physical examination possible; patient responses generally coherent though some hesitancy.
